question:
The following sentence has been split into segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.
I goes to / attend dance classes at / the National Dance Academy.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. I goes to.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "I goes to" contains a subject-verb agreement error. The subject "I" is a first-person singular pronoun, and with first-person singular subjects in the Simple Present Tense, the base form of the verb (V1) is used, not the third-person singular form (V1 + s/es).

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement (Simple Present Tense): With I / we / you / they and plural subjects, use the base verb (go, do, have, etc.). With he / she / it and singular subjects, add -s/-es to the verb (goes, does, has).
◦ Correct: I go to attend dance classes at the National Dance Academy.
◦ Incorrect: I goes to attend dance classes...

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No error" is incorrect because the sentence does contain a grammatical error, as explained above.

• Option 2: "attend dance classes at" is grammatically correct in itself; the infinitive "to attend" correctly follows the corrected verb "go".

• Option 3: "the National Dance Academy." is a correctly formed noun phrase with no grammatical issue.

NOTE

• Common subject-verb agreement errors tested by SSC include wrong use of "is/are", "has/have", and "do/does" with singular/plural subjects.

• Remember: I always takes the base form of the verb in the present tense (I go, I do, I have), even though it is singular — it is an exception to the usual singular-subject rule.

question:
Select the option that corrects the following sentence.
He has broken his leg yesterday.
option_2: He had broke his leg yesterday.
option_3: He have broken his leg yesterday.
option_4: He has broke his leg yesterday.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. He broke his leg yesterday.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The original sentence wrongly uses the Present Perfect Tense ("has broken") with the time expression "yesterday", which denotes a definite, completed point of time in the past.

• Rule — Present Perfect vs Simple Past: The Present Perfect Tense is used for actions with no definite time of occurrence, or actions connecting the past to the present. Definite past time markers such as "yesterday", "last week", "in 2020", "ago" always require the Simple Past Tense.
◦ Correct: He broke his leg yesterday.
◦ Incorrect: He has broken his leg yesterday.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "He had broke his leg yesterday." is incorrect because it mixes the Past Perfect auxiliary "had" with the incorrect past participle form "broke" (the correct past participle is "broken"), and Past Perfect is not needed here since only one past action is described.

• Option 3: "He have broken his leg yesterday." is incorrect both because "have" does not agree with the third-person singular subject "He" (it should be "has"), and because Present Perfect cannot combine with "yesterday".

• Option 4: "He has broke his leg yesterday." is incorrect because it uses the simple past form "broke" instead of the past participle "broken" after "has", and also wrongly retains Present Perfect with "yesterday".

NOTE

• Other definite-time markers that require the Simple Past Tense: "last night", "in 1998", "two days ago", "when I was young".

• Remember the three forms of break: break (V1) – broke (V2) – broken (V3).

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
I noticed that they / did not went to / the museum but entered / a shopping complex.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. did not went to.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "did not went to" is incorrect because the auxiliary "did" must always be followed by the base form (V1) of the main verb, never by the past form (V2).

• Rule — Negative Simple Past: Subject + did not + V1 + Object.
◦ Correct: They did not go to the museum.
◦ Incorrect: They did not went to the museum.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "the museum but entered" is grammatically correct; "entered" (Simple Past) correctly matches the tense of the rest of the sentence.

• Option 3: "a shopping complex." is a correctly formed noun phrase with no grammatical fault.

• Option 4: "I noticed that they" is correct; "noticed" is the correct Simple Past form of "notice", correctly introducing the noun clause.

NOTE

• This is one of the most frequently tested SSC error-spotting rules: once "did/does/do" appears as an auxiliary in a question or negative sentence, the main verb always reverts to its base form.

• Similar structures to watch for: "did not go" (not "did not went"), "did not see" (not "did not saw"), "does not do" (not "does not does").

question:
The given sentence is divided into three segments. Select the option that has the segment with a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.
The meeting was called off / due to a medical emergency of / the manager of the company.
option_4: due to a medical emergency of
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. No error.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The meeting was called off due to a medical emergency of the manager of the company." is grammatically well-formed. The passive voice verb "was called off", the causal preposition phrase "due to", and the possessive chain "of the manager of the company" are all correctly constructed.

• Rule — "Due to": "Due to" is a compound preposition meaning "caused by", and it is correctly used here to introduce the reason for the meeting being called off.

• Since none of the three segments contains any error of tense, agreement, preposition, or word order, the correct choice is "No error".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "the manager of the company." is a correctly formed possessive noun phrase; there is no fault here.

• Option 3: "The meeting was called off" is a correct passive-voice construction (was + past participle) with correct subject-verb agreement.

• Option 4: "due to a medical emergency of" correctly uses the preposition "due to" followed by a noun phrase; there is no grammatical fault.

NOTE

• In error-spotting questions, always check each segment independently for tense, subject-verb agreement, preposition usage, and word order before concluding "No error".

• Common confusion: "due to" is traditionally used only after a form of "to be" or as an adjective phrase, while "owing to" / "because of" are used to modify verbs directly; in modern usage, however, all three are commonly accepted interchangeably.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

If we look at the global population, out of every six persons living in this world, one is an Indian and (1)______ a Chinese. The population of Pakistan is very (2)_____ and accounts for roughly about one-tenth of China or India. Though China is the largest nation and geographically (3)____ the largest area among the three nations, its density is the lowest. Scholars point out the one child (4)____ in China in the late 1970s as the major reason for low population growth. They also state that this measure led to a (5)_____ in the sex ratio, the proportion of females per 1000 males.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. another.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence states "one is an Indian and (1) a Chinese", comparing two individual persons out of the six. "Another" correctly means "one more, a different one", fitting the sense of introducing a second, distinct person after "one".

• Rule — "another" vs "other" determiners: "Another" is used before a singular countable noun to mean "one more" or "a different one", exactly the sense required here (one person is Indian, another single person is Chinese).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "many" is incorrect because "many" indicates a large plural quantity, which contradicts the sense of a single individual being referred to.

• Option 3: "either" is incorrect because "either" is used to mean "one or the other of two", implying a choice, which does not fit the descriptive, non-choice context of the sentence.

• Option 4: "second" is incorrect because it would require a definite article ("a second" does work grammatically, but it awkwardly implies a strict numerical sequence rather than simply indicating a different individual, making it a weaker fit than "another").

NOTE

• Distinguish: "another" = one more/different (singular); "other" = different (used with plural or with "the"); "others" = pronoun for more of the same kind.

• This distinction between "another", "other", "others" is frequently tested in SSC cloze and error-spotting questions.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

If we look at the global population, out of every six persons living in this world, one is an Indian and (1)______ a Chinese. The population of Pakistan is very (2)_____ and accounts for roughly about one-tenth of China or India. Though China is the largest nation and geographically (3)____ the largest area among the three nations, its density is the lowest. Scholars point out the one child (4)____ in China in the late 1970s as the major reason for low population growth. They also state that this measure led to a (5)_____ in the sex ratio, the proportion of females per 1000 males.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. small.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads "The population of Pakistan is very (2) and accounts for roughly about one-tenth of China or India". Since Pakistan's population is stated to be only about one-tenth of China's or India's, the blank must be filled with a word meaning "comparatively little in size", which "small" correctly conveys.

• Rule — Adjective-noun collocation: "Small" is the natural adjective to describe a population size, and it logically links to the following clause about it being one-tenth of the other countries' populations.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "obscure" is incorrect because it means "not well known or unclear", which does not describe the size of a population.

• Option 3: "much" is incorrect because "much" is generally used with uncountable nouns to indicate a large quantity, and grammatically "very much" before a linking verb like "is" is an unnatural, ill-fitting construction here.

• Option 4: "a little" is incorrect because "a little" functions as a quantifying determiner/adverb (e.g., "a little population" is not idiomatic), and it does not combine naturally with "very" in this construction ("very a little" is ungrammatical).

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always check that the chosen word both fits the intended meaning and forms a grammatically natural collocation with the surrounding words (here, **"very ___"** before a linking verb requires a plain adjective like "small").

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

If we look at the global population, out of every six persons living in this world, one is an Indian and (1)______ a Chinese. The population of Pakistan is very (2)_____ and accounts for roughly about one-tenth of China or India. Though China is the largest nation and geographically (3)____ the largest area among the three nations, its density is the lowest. Scholars point out the one child (4)____ in China in the late 1970s as the major reason for low population growth. They also state that this measure led to a (5)_____ in the sex ratio, the proportion of females per 1000 males.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. occupies.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads "Though China is the largest nation and geographically (3) the largest area among the three nations...". "Occupies" correctly conveys the sense of "covers/takes up" a geographical area, which is the standard collocation used to describe land area.

• Rule — Collocation with "area": The verb that naturally collocates with "area" in the sense of physical geographic extent is "occupy" (e.g., "the country occupies a vast area").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "grasps" is incorrect because "grasp" means to physically seize or to understand mentally, neither of which fits describing a country's land area.

• Option 3: "rents" is incorrect because "rent" means to pay for temporary use of property, which is meaningless in the context of a nation's own geographical territory.

• Option 4: "lodges" is incorrect because "lodge" means to provide temporary accommodation or to formally submit (e.g., a complaint), which does not fit describing land area.

NOTE

• Common SSC cloze collocations: a country "occupies" or "covers" an area; a person "occupies" a position/seat; a building "occupies" a plot of land.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

If we look at the global population, out of every six persons living in this world, one is an Indian and (1)______ a Chinese. The population of Pakistan is very (2)_____ and accounts for roughly about one-tenth of China or India. Though China is the largest nation and geographically (3)____ the largest area among the three nations, its density is the lowest. Scholars point out the one child (4)____ in China in the late 1970s as the major reason for low population growth. They also state that this measure led to a (5)_____ in the sex ratio, the proportion of females per 1000 males.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. statute.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads "Scholars point out the one child (4) in China in the late 1970s as the major reason for low population growth", referring to China's well-known one-child population-control law introduced in the late 1970s. "Statute" means a formal, written law enacted by a governing authority, which correctly describes this official government measure.

• Rule — Word meaning in context: Among the given options, only "statute" denotes a formal rule/law of the kind a government would enact to control population growth.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "average" is incorrect because it means a typical or mean value, which does not describe a government measure or law.

• Option 3: "ordeal" is incorrect because it means a painful or difficult experience, which does not fit the sense of an official government policy/law.

• Option 4: "standard" is incorrect because it means a level of quality or a norm, not a formally enacted rule or law.

NOTE

• "Statute" = a written law passed by a legislative body; distinguish from "statue" (a sculpture) — a commonly confused homophone-like pair in vocabulary questions.

• China's one-child law (in general usage, often called the "one-child policy") was in force from 1980 to 2015.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

If we look at the global population, out of every six persons living in this world, one is an Indian and (1)______ a Chinese. The population of Pakistan is very (2)_____ and accounts for roughly about one-tenth of China or India. Though China is the largest nation and geographically (3)____ the largest area among the three nations, its density is the lowest. Scholars point out the one child (4)____ in China in the late 1970s as the major reason for low population growth. They also state that this measure led to a (5)_____ in the sex ratio, the proportion of females per 1000 males.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. decline.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads "...this measure led to a (5) in the sex ratio, the proportion of females per 1000 males". The blank needs a noun (following the article "a") meaning a gradual decrease, which "decline" correctly provides, matching the well-documented fall in the female-to-male sex ratio in China after the one-child law.

• Rule — Part of speech: Since the blank follows the article "a" and precedes the preposition "in" (**"a ___ in the sex ratio"), a countable/uncountable noun** is grammatically required.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "suspension" is incorrect in meaning; "suspension" means a temporary halt or stoppage, not a gradual fall in a ratio.

• Option 3: "diminish" is incorrect because "diminish" is a verb, not a noun, so it cannot correctly follow the article "a" in this slot.

• Option 4: "failure" is incorrect in meaning; "failure" means an unsuccessful outcome or breakdown, which does not describe a change in a numerical ratio.

NOTE

• Watch for part-of-speech traps in cloze tests: an article (a/an/the) immediately before a blank almost always signals that a noun is required, ruling out verb-only options like "diminish".

• Related noun/verb pairs often tested: decline (n./v.) – decline; diminish (v.) – diminution (n.); increase (n./v.).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Lethargic
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Active.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Lethargic" means feeling sluggish, drowsy, and lacking energy or enthusiasm. (सुस्त, आलसी) Its antonym must express energetic, lively behaviour, which "Active" correctly conveys.
◦ Example: After a good night's sleep, she felt active and ready to start the day, quite unlike her usual lethargic mornings.

• Rule — Antonym matching: Always match the antonym to the exact sense of the given word — here, "lethargic" concerns physical/mental energy level, so the antonym must also concern energy level, not intelligence or appearance.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Exhausted" (थका हुआ): Means extremely tired, which is actually close in meaning to lethargic (a lack of energy), not its opposite.

• Option 2: "Intelligent" (बुद्धिमान): Relates to mental sharpness, not physical energy or alertness, so it is not a true antonym of "lethargic".

• Option 4: "Cute" (प्यारा): Relates to physical appearance/charm, which is unrelated to the concept of energy level.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "lethargic": sluggish, listless, languid, torpid, drowsy.

• Other antonym pairs based on energy level often asked by SSC: lazy ↔ diligent/industrious, languid ↔ vigorous, dormant ↔ active.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Please take many as you want.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. as much.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence requires the fixed correlative structure "as much as", which is used to indicate an unspecified quantity equal to one's need or desire. Also, "many" in the original sentence is grammatically wrong because it should agree with an uncountable quantity implied by "take ... as you want", corrected by the countable-neutral phrase "as much".

• Rule — "as much as": The correlative pair "as much as" is used with uncountable nouns/implied quantities to mean "an amount equal to", as in "Take as much as you want/like/need".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "so much" is incorrect because "so much" is typically used in statements of degree/result (e.g., "He ate so much that he felt sick") or in negative/comparative constructions, not in this correlative "as ... as" structure.

• Option 3: "too much" is incorrect because "too much" implies an excessive quantity, which changes and distorts the intended meaning of taking an amount matching one's want.

• Option 4: "much of" is incorrect because "much of" is followed by a noun phrase (e.g., "much of the work") and does not fit grammatically before "as you want".

NOTE

• Common fixed phrases tested by SSC: "as much as", "as many as", "so much that", "too much for".

• "Many" is used with countable nouns and "much" with uncountable nouns; in the fixed idiom "take as much/many as you want", the choice depends on whether the object being taken is countable or uncountable.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the bracketed word in the following sentence to fill in the blank.
The city's infrastructure was ill-equipped to handle the influx of ________(visitors) during the peak season.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. tourists.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Visitors" means people who come to a place temporarily, especially for sightseeing or leisure. (आगंतुक/यात्री) In the context of "peak season" and "influx", "tourists" — people visiting a place for travel/leisure — is the closest synonym.
◦ Example: During the peak season, the hill station is flooded with tourists from across the country.

• Rule — Contextual synonym: The correct synonym must fit both the dictionary meaning of the bracketed word and the surrounding context (here, "peak season" strongly signals travel-related visitors, i.e., tourists).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "citizens" (नागरिक): Refers to legal members/inhabitants of a country or city, not temporary visitors, so it does not fit "peak season influx".

• Option 3: "natives" (मूल निवासी): Refers to people born in a particular place, the opposite sense of an outside visitor.

• Option 4: "residents" (निवासी): Refers to people who permanently live in a place, again the opposite of a temporary visitor.

NOTE

• Commonly confused set: visitor/tourist (temporary, from outside) vs resident/native/citizen/inhabitant (permanent, belonging to the place) — a frequently tested vocabulary distinction in SSC exams.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Both the criminals were cruel and ________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. brutal.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Brutal" means savagely violent or merciless. (क्रूर, निर्दयी) It is a near-synonym of "cruel", and the conjunction "and" here joins two words of similar meaning to intensify the description of the criminals.
◦ Example: The dictator was known for his cruel and brutal treatment of political prisoners.

• Rule — Coordinating conjunction "and": When two adjectives are joined by "and" to describe the same subject, they typically share a similar or complementary meaning/tone (here, both negative), rather than being contradictory.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "sympathetic" (सहानुभूतिपूर्ण): Means kind and compassionate, which is the opposite of "cruel" and cannot logically be joined to it by "and".

• Option 2: "warm" (स्नेहपूर्ण): Means friendly and affectionate, again contradicting the negative sense of "cruel".

• Option 4: "diligent" (मेहनती): Means hardworking and careful, which is unrelated in meaning to "cruel" and does not fit the intended sense of describing the criminals' harsh nature.

NOTE

• Words related to "cruel"/"brutal" often tested: ruthless, merciless, savage, ferocious, barbaric, sadistic.

• Antonyms of "cruel": kind, gentle, compassionate, humane, benevolent.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the following sentence.
Rimjhim received a children's very illustrated colourful atlas on her 10th birthday.
option_1: a very illustrated colourful atlas children
option_2: a very colourful illustrated children's atlas
option_3: an very illustrated colourful children's atlas
option_4: a colourful very illustrated children's atlas
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. a very colourful illustrated children's atlas.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The original phrase "a children's very illustrated colourful atlas" wrongly places the possessive noun modifier "children's" before the descriptive adjectives, and separates the intensifier "very" from the adjective it should logically modify.

• Rule — Order of Adjectives: In English, the standard order before a noun is: Determiner → Opinion → Size → Age → Shape → Colour → Origin → Material → Purpose/Noun-modifier → Head Noun. Here, "very colourful" (a descriptive quality with its intensifier) and "illustrated" (a descriptive/type adjective) should come before the purpose-indicating possessive noun-modifier "children's", which sits closest to the head noun "atlas".
◦ Correct order: a very colourful illustrated children's atlas.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "a very illustrated colourful atlas children" is incorrect because it wrongly places "children" at the end, disconnected from its possessive form, which is ungrammatical.

• Option 3: "an very illustrated colourful children's atlas" is incorrect because the article "an" is used before "very", which begins with a consonant sound; the correct article is "a".

• Option 4: "a colourful very illustrated children's atlas" is incorrect because the intensifier "very" is misplaced — it should directly precede the adjective it intensifies ("colourful"), i.e., "very colourful", not split as "colourful very illustrated".

NOTE

• Standard adjective order mnemonic: Opinion, Size, Age, Shape, Colour, Origin, Material, Purpose (OSASCOMP).

• Possessive noun-modifiers (like "children's", "boy's") typically sit closest to the noun they modify, just before the head noun.

question:
Identify the incorrectly spelt word and select its correct spelling.
Wether we want to admit it or not, we all wish everyone would like us.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. whether.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Wether" as printed in the sentence is misspelt. The correct spelling is "Whether", meaning used to introduce a choice or doubt between alternatives.

• Spelling key: WH + ETHER. The word begins with the digraph "wh-" (as in "when", "where", "why"), followed by "ether".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "addmit" is incorrect; the word "admit" (the correct spelling appearing later in the sentence) has only one "d", not a double "dd".

• Option 3: "admitt" is incorrect; the correct spelling "admit" ends with a single "t", not a double "tt".

• Option 4: "whither" is incorrect as a substitute here; "whither" is a distinct, archaic word meaning "to what place", not a misspelling of "whether" — it is a different word entirely and does not fit the sentence's meaning.

NOTE

• Commonly confused near-homophones: whether (introducing a choice) vs weather (climatic condition) vs whither (to what place, archaic).

• Other "wh-" spelling words frequently tested: wheel, wheat, whistle, wharf, whim.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Slip your mind
option_2: Think about something for a short time
option_4: Can't think of anything to say
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Forget about something.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Slip your mind" means to be forgotten by you, especially something you intended to do or remember. (भूल जाना) It is used when someone unintentionally forgets a task, appointment, or piece of information.
◦ Example: I meant to call you back, but it completely slipped my mind.

• The idiom draws on the image of something "slipping away" or "sliding out" of one's mind, just as a physical object might slip out of one's grasp.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: To think about something for a short time (थोड़ी देर सोचना): This describes a brief moment of thought, not forgetting, and does not match the idiom's meaning.

• Option 3: To immediately think of something (तुरंत याद आना): This is closer to "cross one's mind" or "come to mind", the opposite sense of forgetting.

• Option 4: Can't think of anything to say (कुछ कहने के लिए न सूझना): This describes being at a loss for words, which is a different idiom altogether (e.g., "lost for words"), not "slip your mind".

NOTE

• Related idioms of memory often asked in SSC: "cross one's mind" (to occur to someone), "on the tip of one's tongue" (almost remembered but not quite recalled), "ring a bell" (to sound familiar), "draw a blank" (to fail to remember).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
I was in the _________ of a meeting when somebody called me.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. middle.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The fixed idiomatic phrase "in the middle of" means in the process of doing something, or at a point partway through an activity. (किसी काम के बीच में) It correctly conveys that the speaker was interrupted while a meeting was ongoing.
◦ Example: She was in the middle of cooking dinner when the power went out.

• Rule — Fixed collocation: English idiomatically uses "in the middle of" (not "centre", "corner" or "round") to describe being interrupted during an ongoing activity or event.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "centre", while a near-synonym of "middle" in a purely spatial sense, is not used in this fixed idiomatic collocation "in the ___ of a meeting" to describe being interrupted mid-activity.

• Option 2: "corner" is incorrect because it refers to a spatial location (an edge/angle), not a point in the progress of an activity.

• Option 3: "round" is incorrect because it does not idiomatically combine with "in the ___ of" to indicate being partway through an event.

NOTE

• Other fixed phrases with "middle" tested by SSC: "in the middle of nowhere" (in a very remote place), "middle-aged", "middle ground" (a compromise position).

question:
Select the most appropriate spelling of the underlined word in the given sentence.
The prison is euphemistically called a 'rehabillitation centre'.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. rehabilitation.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "rehabillitation" is misspelt. The correct spelling is "rehabilitation" — the process of restoring someone to a normal, useful life through training or therapy.

• Spelling key: RE + HABILITATE + ION → REHABILITATION. Note there is only a single "l" in the middle of the word, not a double "ll".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "rehabilition" is incorrect; it wrongly drops the "ta" before the ending, giving "-ilition" instead of the correct "-ilitation".

• Option 3: "rehbilitation" is incorrect; it wrongly drops the "a" after "reh-", giving "rehb-" instead of the correct "rehab-".

• Option 4: "rehabilation" is incorrect; it wrongly drops the "it" before the ending, giving "-abilation" instead of the correct "-abilitation".

NOTE

• The root word is "habilitate" (from Latin habilis, meaning "fit, able"), with the prefix "re-" meaning "again".

• Related words with double letters commonly confused by test-takers: occasion, necessary, embarrass, accommodate — always check whether a consonant is single or double.

question:
Identify the most appropriate synonym of the following word.
Implicate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Accuse.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Implicate" means to show or indicate that someone is involved in a crime or wrongdoing. (फंसाना, दोषी ठहराना) "Accuse" is its closest synonym, as both words involve pointing to someone's involvement in wrongdoing.
◦ Example: The witness's testimony implicated three other people in the fraud.

• Rule — Contextual synonym matching: Focus on the core sense of "involvement in wrongdoing/blame" — among the options, only "accuse" shares this sense with "implicate".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Complain" (शिकायत करना): Means to express dissatisfaction, unrelated to indicating someone's guilt or involvement.

• Option 2: "Confuse" (उलझाना): Means to cause bewilderment or lack of understanding, which is unrelated to accusing or blaming someone.

• Option 4: "Interrogate" (पूछताछ करना): Means to question someone formally, which is a related but distinct action from "implicating" (showing involvement); one can interrogate someone without implicating them, and vice versa.

NOTE

• Related words: implicate (verb) → implication (noun) → implicated (adjective).

• Commonly confused pair: implicate (to involve in wrongdoing) vs implicit (implied, not directly stated) — these look similar but have very different meanings.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the word given in brackets to fill in the blank.
The firefighter summoned all her _________ (cowardice) and rushed into the burning building.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. courage.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Cowardice" means a lack of bravery; a tendency to avoid danger or pain out of fear. (कायरता) Its direct antonym is "courage", meaning the ability to face danger or fear without being deterred. (साहस)

• Rule — Contextual fit: The sentence describes the firefighter rushing into a burning building, an act requiring bravery, which logically requires the antonym of "cowardice", i.e., "courage", not skill or knowledge.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "skills" (कौशल): Refers to competence or ability to perform a task, not the emotional quality of bravery, so it is not the antonym of "cowardice".

• Option 2: "erudition" (विद्वता): Means extensive knowledge gained from study, unrelated to bravery or fear.

• Option 4: "expertise" (विशेषज्ञता): Means specialised skill or knowledge in a particular field, again unrelated to the emotional quality of courage versus cowardice.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "cowardice": timidity, faintheartedness, spinelessness.

• Synonyms of "courage": bravery, valour, fortitude, gallantry, boldness — frequently tested SSC vocabulary.

question:
Select the most appropriate homonym to fill in the blank.
__________is a red-coloured root vegetable.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Beet.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Beet" refers to a red-coloured root vegetable, commonly known as beetroot, used in salads and cooking. It is a homonym (specifically a homophone) of "beat", meaning to strike repeatedly or to defeat.

• Rule — Homonyms/Homophones: Words that sound alike but have different meanings and often different spellings are called homophones. Here, the sentence's meaning (a vegetable) determines that the correct spelling is "Beet", not its sound-alike "Beat".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Beat" means to strike repeatedly or to defeat someone in a contest; it does not refer to a vegetable.

• Option 3: "Bead" refers to a small, decorative ball with a hole for threading, unrelated to a vegetable, and it is not even a homophone of "beet".

• Option 4: "Bit" refers to a small piece or amount of something (or the past tense of "bite"); it is unrelated to a vegetable and not a homophone of "beet" either.

NOTE

• Other commonly tested homophone pairs in SSC exams: beet/beat, bare/bear, flour/flower, sea/see, meat/meet, peace/piece.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Pliable
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Malleable.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Pliable" means easily bent or shaped; flexible, or easily influenced/adaptable. (लचीला) "Malleable" is its closest synonym, meaning capable of being shaped or influenced.
◦ Example: Young minds are often pliable/malleable and easily influenced by their surroundings.

• Rule — Synonym matching: Both "pliable" and "malleable" convey the sense of physical or figurative flexibility/adaptability, making them close synonyms.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Severe" (कठोर): Means harsh or strict, which is unrelated to flexibility and is closer to the opposite sense.

• Option 2: "Probable" (संभावित): Means likely to happen, an entirely unrelated meaning concerning likelihood, not flexibility.

• Option 4: "Rigid" (कठोर, अटल): Means stiff and inflexible, which is actually the antonym of "pliable", not its synonym.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "pliable": flexible, supple, adaptable, ductile.

• Antonyms of "pliable": rigid, stiff, inflexible, unyielding — a commonly tested pair alongside its synonyms.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Lose heart
option_1: To be suspicious of your success
option_2: To get success by believing in yourself
option_3: To stop believing that you can succeed
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. To stop believing that you can succeed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Lose heart" means to become discouraged or disheartened; to lose confidence or hope of succeeding. (हिम्मत हारना)
◦ Example: Despite failing the exam twice, she did not lose heart and kept trying until she succeeded.

• The idiom uses "heart" figuratively to represent courage and hope, so "losing" one's heart means losing the will or confidence to continue.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: To be suspicious of your success (अपनी सफलता पर संदेह करना): This describes doubt about a specific outcome rather than a general loss of hope/confidence, and does not match the idiom.

• Option 2: To get success by believing in yourself (खुद पर विश्वास करके सफलता पाना): This is nearly the opposite meaning — gaining success through confidence, not losing hope.

• Option 4: To believe in your success (अपनी सफलता में विश्वास रखना): This is the direct opposite of "losing heart", which describes losing (not gaining) confidence.

NOTE

• The opposite idiom is "take heart", meaning to become encouraged or to regain confidence.

• Other "heart" idioms often tested by SSC: "by heart" (from memory), "heart of gold" (a very kind nature), "set one's heart on" (to want something very much), "break someone's heart" (to cause deep sadness).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined words in the following sentence.
I hope you have enjoying yourselves at the party tonight!
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. enjoy yourselves.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb phrase "have enjoying" is grammatically wrong — it incorrectly mixes the auxiliary "have" with the present participle "enjoying" without a proper auxiliary structure. Since the sentence expresses a hope about an ongoing/future event ("tonight"), the Simple Present Tense is idiomatically used after verbs of hoping/wishing for present or near-future situations.

• Rule — Verbs of hope/wish + Simple Present: After "I hope (that)...", when referring to a present or future situation, the Simple Present Tense form of the verb is used, e.g., "I hope you enjoy yourselves", "I hope it rains tomorrow".

• The reflexive pronoun must also agree with the subject "you" (referring to multiple people at the party), so "yourselves" (plural reflexive) is correctly retained.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "enjoys yourselves" is incorrect because "enjoys" (third-person singular) does not agree with the subject "you", and reflexive pronoun "yourselves" also mismatches a singular verb form.

• Option 2: "will be enjoy himself" is incorrect because it uses the wrong auxiliary structure ("will be enjoy" is not a valid tense form; it should be "will be enjoying" or "will enjoy"), and the reflexive pronoun "himself" wrongly refers to a third-person singular subject instead of "you" (plural).

• Option 3: "are enjoying themselves" is incorrect because "themselves" does not agree with the subject "you"; it should be "yourselves", and it also incorrectly shifts to third person.

NOTE

• Reflexive pronouns must always agree in person and number with their subject: I – myself, you (sing./pl.) – yourself/yourselves, he – himself, she – herself, it – itself, we – ourselves, they – themselves.

• Verbs like hope, wish, trust followed by a present/future time reference typically take the Simple Present Tense in the subordinate clause, not the Present Perfect or a mixed auxiliary form.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Their was a large snake found in the garden last evening.
option_3: There was not a large snake
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. There was a large snake.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined segment wrongly uses "Their" (a possessive pronoun/determiner) instead of "There" (used to introduce the existence of something). Since the sentence is describing the existence of a snake in the garden, the correct existential construction "There was..." must be used.

• Rule — "There is/was" (existential construction): "There + be-verb" is used to state that something exists or happened at a place, e.g., "There was a large snake found in the garden." "Their", by contrast, is a possessive form meaning "belonging to them" and cannot be used to begin an existential sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "There was the larger snake" is incorrect because "the larger snake" wrongly uses the comparative form "larger" (implying a comparison between two snakes) and the definite article "the" (implying a specific, already-known snake), whereas the original sentence introduces the snake for the first time with the indefinite article "a" and the simple adjective "large".

• Option 3: "There was not a large snake" is incorrect because it introduces a negative ("not"), completely reversing the meaning of the original sentence, which states that a snake was found.

• Option 4: "Their was the larger snake" is incorrect because it retains the original error ("Their" instead of "There") and additionally introduces the incorrect comparative/definite phrasing "the larger snake".

NOTE

• Commonly confused homophones: there (place/existential use), their (possessive), they're (contraction of "they are") — one of the most frequently tested confusions in SSC error-spotting and sentence-improvement questions.

• Use the indefinite article "a" when introducing a noun for the first time, and the definite article "the" only when referring back to something already known/specific.
